title: Recommended Next Steps on Artificial Intelligence and Teaching (memorandum to Suffolk Law faculty)
author: Andrew Perlman

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source addresses law-student AI use, learning effects and school policies rather than direct-to-consumer legal assistance or access-to-justice risks. Its task-dependent caution is broadly compatible with the cluster, but it provides insufficient evidence to determine a position on the cluster’s principal proposition.

st.t: AI curriculum: Assistance must preserve intellectual development
st.an: The memorandum accepts that AI instruction must preserve independent legal reasoning and materially develops that proposition with task-specific experimental evidence, differentiated institutional approaches, and safeguards for faculty policy, assessment and student training. It distinguishes improved AI-assisted work from durable learning and recommends use that reinforces rather than shortcuts intellectual development.
qs: Finally, we need to examine the training and resources we offer students so that they can use AI in ways that reinforce learning rather than shortcut it.

st.t: AI instruction: Timing divides educational reform
st.an: Perlman accepts the cluster’s central framing that legal education must develop independent judgment and AI competence together, while adding a concrete, context-specific reform program: separate treatment of AI literacy, student use, faculty use and assessment; mixed-evidence analysis; differentiated restrictions; and temporary, revisable safeguards.
qs: In short, a simple “AI is good” perspective fails to account for ways in which unfettered AI use could undermine our educational mission, and a simple “AI is bad” perspective may do our students a disservice by failing to prepare them for the profession they will enter.
We need an evidence-informed, context-specific, and revisable approach to AI’s role in our educational mission.

st.t: Judgment development: AI exposure is not professional readiness
st.an: Perlman accepts the cluster’s core distinction between AI exposure and professional readiness, while materially extending it through a coordinated, revisable institutional framework that separates learning about and with AI from teaching and assessment. He also grounds that framework in conditional experimental findings and proposes differentiated coursework rules, controlled assessments, AI-literacy review and temporary safeguards rather than blanket permission or prohibition.
qs: We need an evidence-informed, context-specific, and revisable approach to AI’s role in our educational mission.

st.t: Law-school policy: Staged use bridges bans and adoption
st.an: Suffolk accepts the cluster’s staged middle path and materially develops it through differentiated rules by course level, learning objective and work stage, alongside process-based assessments, disclosure, human review and revisable interim safeguards.
qs: We need an evidence-informed, context-specific, and revisable approach to AI’s role in our educational mission.
Options may include staged submissions, process            documentation, oral discussion or defense, expressly AI-permitted assignments,            and disclosure of authorized AI use.

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: The memorandum accepts the cluster’s task-specific view of AI capability and materially extends its educational implications: it cites controlled evidence of quality gains on several defined legal tasks, reports a separate task-level benchmark, and urges faculty to reassess newer systems while recognizing that use can support or undermine learning. It does not establish autonomous professional competence or resolve the cluster’s access-to-justice and protection-boundary questions.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Perlman accepts the cluster’s core view that AI produces meaningful but context-dependent gains while creating competence and learning risks that require human accountability. He materially develops it through a concrete law-school framework: differentiated AI rules by course and task, protected foundational learning, controlled assessments, curriculum review, disclosure, training, and temporary safeguards subject to evidence-based revision.
qs: We need an evidence-informed, context-specific, and revisable approach to AI’s role in our educational mission.

st.t: Professional governance: Existing duties need active AI scrutiny
st.an: The memorandum accepts the cluster’s core view that responsible AI adoption requires active institutional governance and competence-building. It materially develops that proposition for legal education through controlled assessments, pedagogical experimentation, protection of foundational learning, and an evidence-informed policy process designed for continuing revision.
qs: We need an evidence-informed, context-specific, and revisable approach to AI’s role in our educational mission.

We may similarly wish to use controlled conditions for some assessments and redesign some outside writing assignments (assessing in an AI world), while at the same time encouraging faculty to explore how AI might improve pedagogy and expand opportunities for formative assessments (teaching with AI).

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The memorandum accepts the cluster’s supervised-AI model by requiring human responsibility, substantive verification and controlled handling of protected information. It materially extends that proposition into legal education through curriculum reform, AI-literacy instruction and preservation of foundational competencies needed to evaluate AI output independently.

We must continue teaching these and other foundational competencies.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The memorandum accepts the need for selective, human-led AI deployment and concretely extends it to legal education through mandatory verification, faculty accountability, controlled experimentation, disclosure and assessment redesign. Its safeguards operationalise the cluster’s claims that nominal human involvement is insufficient and that value and safety depend on use-context-specific workflow design.

Faculty who find AI pedagogically useful should develop carefully designed experiments, subject to the cautions above.

st.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure
st.an: The memorandum supports the cluster’s distinction between task-specific AI capability, beneficial human assistance and broader professional performance. It cites bounded gains in student work and selected legal tasks while expressly making educational value dependent on the use case; it does not establish dependable autonomous lawyering or complete-task reliability.

kp.k: Legal education needs differentiated, revisable AI policies
kp.d: Perlman recommends distinguishing learning about AI, learning with AI, teaching with AI, and assessment. Preparing students to use professional tools may justify mandatory AI instruction while protecting foundational competence may justify restrictions on student use, particularly in first-year courses. This is a proposed educational response, not a finding that one policy is universally effective.
qs: We need an evidence-informed, context-specific, and revisable approach to AI’s role in our educational mission.
The former approach prepares our students to use the tools they will encounter, while the latter ensures that they develop the sophistication to use the tools effectively.

kp.k: Reported studies show stronger AI-assisted legal work
kp.d: The memo cites a randomized controlled study of 137 upper-level students at Minnesota and Michigan in which retrieval-augmented generation and a reasoning model improved work-product quality on at least four of six tasks against no-AI controls. Separately, it reports that the February 27, 2025 Vals AI industry benchmark found an AI product matched or exceeded its lawyer baseline on five of seven tasks. These are reported study and benchmark results, distinct from Perlman's broader assertion that capabilities have subsequently improved.
qs: In a randomized controlled study involving 137 upper- level law students at the University of Minnesota and the University of Michigan, newer AI tools (using a retrieval-augmented generation platform and an AI reasoning model) improved work-product quality on at least four of six tasks relative to no-AI controls.

A 2025 industry benchmark similarly reported that an AI product matched or exceeded the report’s lawyer baseline on five of the seven assigned tasks: data extraction, document question answering, document summarization, transcript analysis, and chronology generation.

kp.k: Professors preferred AI answers, without establishing learning gains
kp.d: The memo reports a 2026 Stanford-led unpublished study involving sixteen contracts professors from fourteen law schools, forty representative office-hours questions, and blind comparisons with professor-drafted answers. Professors preferred AI answers roughly three-quarters of the time and rated them potentially harmful less often, approximately 3.5% versus 12%. Perlman expressly limits the inference to relative preference and perceived harmfulness, not objective accuracy or learning outcomes.
qs: The authors found that the professors preferred the AI- generated answers roughly three-quarters of the time and rated them as potentially harmful to student learning less often than they rated their colleagues’ answers (approximately 3.5% versus 12%).
(The forced-choice design measured relative preference and perceived harmfulness, not objective doctrinal accuracy or student learning.)

kp.k: AI literacy should complement foundational professional competencies
kp.d: Perlman argues that lawyers using AI must understand its capabilities and limitations while retaining traditional legal skills. Suffolk's technology and innovation offerings remain largely optional, apart from Legal Practice Skills instruction and requirements for LIT concentrators. He recommends evaluating additional mandatory training, including a required one-credit AI-literacy course for 1Ls alongside a proposed sixth LPS credit, with curricular recommendations in spring 2027 rather than announcing adoption.
qs: Future lawyers will continue to need the traditional competencies we have long taught, including problem solving, negotiation, effective written and oral advocacy, client counseling, fact investigation, and analytical and strategic thinking.
The retreat also identified a concrete question: whether to add a required one-credit AI-literacy course for 1Ls.
The Curriculum Committee should evaluate that possibility alongside the sixth LPS credit already under consideration by the LPS Committee.

kp.k: Student AI use is already widespread
kp.d: Citing the Thomson Reuters Institute's 2026 Law Student Pulse Survey, the memo reports that almost six in ten of more than 1,800 surveyed law students used AI at least several times weekly for academic work. It describes possible uses including outlines, explanations, practice questions, feedback, simulated Socratic dialogue and podcasts; these examples are not presented as separately quantified survey findings. Such practices raise learning, copyright, licensing, consent and privacy questions.
qs: A 2026 survey of more than 1,800 law students found that almost six in ten used AI at least several times per week for academic work.

In addition to the questions about copyright, licensing, consent, and privacy that these practices raise, there are many unsettled questions about the extent to which these uses help or harm learning.

kp.k: AI's learning effects depend on use conditions
kp.d: The memo cites a 2026 randomized controlled study of ninety-one second- and third-year Minnesota law students completing a structured four-stage exercise. Initial AI access improved work and speed without reducing subsequent unaided comprehension and reasoning, contrary to the researchers' hypothesis. When everyone used AI for revision, weaker initial drafts improved while stronger drafts regressed. Perlman cautions against treating AI as either inevitably deskilling or reliably educational.
qs: Students with access to AI produced stronger initial work more quickly, but contrary to the researchers’ hypothesis, their early AI use did not reduce later unaided performance.
At the revision stage, when all students used AI, students who began with weaker drafts improved while those who began with stronger drafts regressed.
The study counsels against assuming that AI either inevitably erodes or reliably builds legal reasoning; effects may depend on the task, user, timing, and manner of use.

kp.k: Peer schools illustrate divergent educational responses
kp.d: Perlman reports Berkeley's summer 2026 restrictive default on AI in credited work, examinations and uploaded course materials, subject to written instructor departures; Texas's June 2026 integration of AI objectives into selected courses and required practical training, alongside renewed Socratic engagement; and Chicago's 2026–27 AI-resilient pilot. Chicago combines required-core 1L device restrictions and examinations without internet or file access, limited exceptions, selective AI use in writing, oral discussion of substantial research papers beginning with rising 2Ls, and expanded AI instruction. These are other institutions' approaches, not Suffolk's adopted package.
qs: UC Berkeley Law recently adopted a restrictive default for students’ use of AI in coursework.

Dean Bobby Chesney mapped AI learning objectives onto selected for- credit courses and practical AI training sessions within the school’s required Professional Pathways Program, while renewing the emphasis on Socratic, in-class engagement as a setting in which faculty can directly observe students’ reasoning.

Chicago will also restructure its first-year writing program to treat writing without AI as the foundation while using AI at selected stages for research, revision, draft iteration, and oral-argument preparation.

kp.k: Faculty discretion requires informed choices and clear rules
kp.d: Suffolk generally leaves students' AI use to individual faculty, but Perlman argues that this depends on faculty understanding actual student practices and communicating rules. He recommends a school-wide policy differentiated by course level, objectives, work stages and authorized uses, with disclosure expectations and a clear AI definition accounting for embedded features in common software. Proposed interim requirements include an AI policy in every syllabus, stronger orientation and a provisional evidence-informed study guide.
qs: That approach preserves pedagogical discretion, but its effectiveness depends in part on the extent to which faculty know how students use the tools and whether faculty are communicating clear rules.
If either condition is missing, stronger institutional defaults may be warranted.
As an interim step, every syllabus during the coming academic year must state the course’s AI policy: what is permitted, what is prohibited, and under what conditions.

kp.k: AI teaching opportunities require human verification and accountability
kp.d: Perlman identifies potential efficiencies and pedagogical gains in hypotheticals, simulations, model answers, rubrics, assessments, exam-question testing, illustrations and formative feedback at scale. These are conditional possibilities rather than demonstrated Suffolk outcomes. Faculty must review generated teaching content and verify legal propositions and citations; material AI involvement in individualized feedback or evaluation should be disclosed, and faculty retain responsibility. Experimentation is encouraged without an expectation that faculty use AI.
qs: Used thoughtfully, for a defined pedagogical purpose, and with appropriate human review, it may reduce preparation time and improve the quality and consistency of materials offered to students.
It may also make it more feasible to provide additional formative assessment and feedback in larger classes.
Faculty remain responsible for the resulting feedback and evaluation, and an AI output should never be treated as dispositive of a student’s performance.

kp.k: Privacy, confidentiality and access constrain educational AI deployment
kp.d: The memo warns against disclosing identifiable education records to external AI services absent Suffolk approval and FERPA-compliant consent or an applicable exception. It calls for approved services and settings for protected information, opting out of training where available, and attention to clinic-specific duties, copyright and licensing. A proposed interim student rule requires written permission from instructors and every affected student before uploading class recordings or identifiable peer contributions, subject to accommodations and authorized exceptions. The memo also flags bias, over-reliance and unequal access.
qs: Information entered into an AI tool may be retained, reviewed, or used to train models, depending on the product, account type, settings, and current terms.
An instructor’s permission authorizes only uses that the instructor or Suffolk has the legal authority to permit.
Differences in students’ access to and facility with these tools may widen gaps we are working to close.

kp.k: Assessment should distinguish mastery from authorized AI assistance
kp.d: Perlman advises assuming advanced AI access for work outside proctored conditions, while rejecting a universal assessment solution. He recommends reviewing certification, definitions, disclosure and safeguards; separately evaluating in-person administration, proctoring, secure software and closed-book conditions against learning objectives, accessibility, equity and academic freedom; and considering staged submissions, process documentation and oral defenses. Responsible AI-assisted performance can itself be a legitimate assessed competence.
qs: Faculty designing fall assessments should assume that students completing work outside proctored conditions have access to these advanced AI tools.
That capability warrants attention to assessment design, but it does not establish that any single approach (e.g., closed-book exams, oral examinations) is superior for every course.

The committee should not presume that all work completed outside proctored conditions is invalid; in some courses, evaluating responsible AI-assisted work may itself serve an important learning objective.

kp.k: AI detection cannot independently establish student misconduct
kp.d: The proposed assessment review includes investigation standards developed with the Administrative/Disciplinary Committee. Perlman explicitly warns that AI-writing detectors produce both false positives and false negatives and should not alone determine misconduct, distinguishing enforcement evidence from the separate problem of designing robust assessments.
qs: AI-writing detectors can produce false positives and false negatives and should not, standing alone, be treated as dispositive evidence of misconduct.

kp.k: Temporary safeguards precede longer-term faculty policy decisions
kp.d: The memo proposes committee recommendations for spring 2027 and limited interim measures for 2026–27, subject to input and applicable governance. For Civil Procedure, Constitutional Law, Contracts, Criminal Law, Property and Torts, summative assessments would use secure software blocking internet and local files, subject to accommodations, authorized exceptions or deans' approval of a detailed alternative requested at least one month beforehand. Substantial-paper supervisors are invited, not required, to pilot oral defenses or AI-use documentation. Interim assessment measures expire June 30, 2027 or earlier upon superseding faculty-approved policies.
qs: The memo recommends a year of committee work to address each of these four questions in detail, with reports and proposals submitted to the faculty in spring 2027.
They will expire on June 30, 2027, or when superseding faculty- approved policies take effect, whichever occurs first.
The results of these pilots will inform the committee’s work.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Perlman argues that AI can perform increasingly sophisticated legal and educational tasks, requiring changes in professional preparation, teaching, and assessment without abandoning foundational legal competencies.
pts.d: Perlman describes current AI capabilities as including high-performing examination answers, legal scholarship, instructional materials, and assistance with legal work. He argues that lawyers using AI need to understand its capabilities and limitations, while traditional skills such as advocacy, counseling, investigation, and strategic thinking remain necessary. His educational claims are conditional: AI can support or undermine learning depending on its use; thoughtful, human-reviewed faculty use may reduce preparation time, improve materials, and expand formative feedback. He also identifies risks of inaccurate or fabricated content, privacy and confidentiality breaches, bias, over-reliance, and unequal access. AI's ability to complete take-home work creates a need to reconsider assessment design, but he does not claim that all unproctored work is invalid or that one assessment format is universally best. He predicts that disclosure of light AI editing may soon become unnecessary as such assistance becomes assumed.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Perlman supports his claims with cited experiments, a vendor evaluation, a student survey, professional ethics authorities, and institutional experience, while explicitly qualifying what some studies establish.
pts.d: The memo reports a randomized study of 137 upper-level law students in which retrieval-augmented and reasoning-model assistance improved work-product quality on at least four of six tasks. It cites the February 2025 Vals AI report as finding that an AI product matched or exceeded the report's lawyer baseline on five of seven tasks; this is a benchmark result, not evidence of wholesale lawyer replacement. A cited unpublished 2026 study involved sixteen contracts professors from fourteen schools comparing answers to forty representative office-hours questions: professors preferred AI answers roughly three-quarters of the time and judged them potentially harmful less frequently, but the design did not measure objective accuracy or learning. A separate randomized study of ninety-one second- and third-year students found faster, stronger initial AI-assisted work and no reduction in later unaided performance; AI-assisted revision improved weaker drafts but worsened stronger ones. A survey of more than 1,800 students reported frequent academic AI use by almost six in ten. Perlman also cites work on examination performance and AI-generated scholarship, ABA Formal Opinion 512, Massachusetts competence rules, and Suffolk's curricular experience. His forecasts about educational transformation and disclosure norms are author judgments rather than quantified findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The July 27, 2026 memo describes present capabilities and near-term institutional responses, with learning effects and benefits contingent on context, supervision, and tool choice.
pts.d: Perlman draws primarily on 2025–2026 evidence and states that capabilities have improved since the cited studies. He urges attention to leading systems at their most capable settings rather than generalizing from early or free versions. Learning effects are qualified by task, user, timing, and manner of use; teaching benefits require defined pedagogical purposes and human review. Privacy and confidentiality risks depend on product, account, settings, terms, and institutional authorization. The proposed committee work runs through the 2026–27 academic year, with recommendations in spring 2027. Proposed interim measures are subject to input and relevant approvals, and expire on June 30, 2027 unless extended, replaced, or superseded under the stated provisions. The proposal for secure examination software includes accommodation and authorized-exception provisions. These are institutional proposals, not evidence that a particular intervention has already improved learning.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are law students, future lawyers, faculty, and law-school administrators; the memo does not make concrete forecasts about law-firm staffing, pricing, or market displacement.
pts.d: Students face both new learning opportunities and risks to independent judgment, privacy, equity, and the integrity of performance measures. First-year students are a particular focus for foundational learning and controlled assessments; students writing substantial papers may encounter oral defenses or AI-use documentation pilots. Future lawyers need both traditional professional competencies and responsible AI literacy. Faculty may gain assistance with preparation, simulations, assessment materials, and feedback, but retain responsibility for accuracy and evaluation. Administrators and committees must develop curriculum, disclosure, assessment, enforcement, and approved-service policies. Clinical faculty and students have additional confidentiality obligations. The memo notes professional opportunities associated with Suffolk's technology-oriented curriculum but does not quantify employment effects or predict lawyer displacement.
